title: The Effect of Clarity on Learning: Impacting Motivation Through Cognitive Load https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03634523.2023.2250883
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 19, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers a study by Serki and Bolkan testing whether teacher clarity affects learning directly or indirectly, through reduced cognitive load and increased motivation. In an experiment with 252 students comparing structured versus unstructured lessons on social cognitive theory, clearer lessons produced higher test scores via a specific chain: lower cognitive load led to improved self-efficacy and motivation, which then produced better learning outcomes. Barton highlights the study's 'double jeopardy' framing of unclear instruction: it doesn't just make material harder to understand, it simultaneously demotivates students rather than prompting them to compensate with extra effort. He translates the structural findings into classroom moves — organizational cues, breaking down dense paragraphs, headings and numbering, avoiding jargon, and using concrete examples — as accessible ways to reduce extraneous load and, indirectly, lift motivation.
points: Clarity's benefit to learning runs through an indirect chain: clearer instruction reduces cognitive load, which raises self-efficacy and motivation, which then improves outcomes — not a direct clarity-to-achievement link.

Unclear instruction produces a “double jeopardy” effect: it makes material harder to learn AND demotivates students, rather than students compensating with extra effort as unclear material gets harder.

Concrete clarity tools — organizational cues, breaking down complex paragraphs, headings and numbering — are what convert the abstract idea of “being clear” into something teachers can actually implement.
The effect of a single clear lesson was modest in this artificial, text-based experiment, implying that clarity's real payoff is likely cumulative across many lessons rather than a one-off fix.
quotes: When teachers are unclear, they make the material harder for students to learn and, instead of putting in extra effort to compensate, students also become less motivated to learn.
Results supported the hypothesis, showing clearer lessons led to higher test scores via lower cognitive load and improved self-efficacy and motivation.
Teachers should be mindful that unclear instruction can have a detrimental "double jeopardy" effect on students.
Reducing cognitive load not only improves students' ability to learn but also enhances their motivation to learn.
Teachers can achieve this by incorporating organizational cues, breaking down complex paragraphs, and using visual aids like headings and numbering.
